title: Clause 14
setting: A client and legal counsel discuss a late delivery.

lines.t: They're six weeks late. I want to cancel and claim damages.
They'll argue force majeure. The factory flooded.
So we're stuck?
Not necessarily. Clause 14 requires written notice within forty-eight hours.
And they said nothing for eleven days.
That's the point that matters. The delay might be excusable, the silence isn't.
Do we go to court?
I'd settle out of court. Litigation costs more than the invoice.
What would a fair settlement look like?
A credit against the next order, and we amend the notice clause.

title: The version they sent back
setting: A supplier has returned the contract with four quiet changes in it.

lines.t: They've sent the contract back with four changes.
Which clause worries you most?
The termination clause. They want thirty days, we asked for ninety.
A thirty-day notice period on a two-year supply contract is very short.
They call it flexibility.
Then amend it to sixty and give one sentence of reason.
They've also added force majeure covering 'supplier difficulties'.
Force majeure means floods and wars. A late lorry is ordinary business.
And the governing law?
Bulgarian. If it says English law, everything they do wrong costs you a London solicitor.
What about the waiver they slipped into the terms and conditions?
Take it out. Give up a right once and you'll be asked to give it up every year after.
So until this is signed, everything stays subject to contract?
Correct. Nothing is binding yet, any promise made this week is void unless it's in the document, and every breach of contract argument starts with what's written.

title: Before you write back
setting: A two-line email that could turn into something larger.

lines.t: Can I answer their email myself?
Write it, then send it to me before it goes.
It's two lines.
Two lines is how most disputes start.
Should I mark it 'without prejudice'?
Only if you're making an offer to settle. It keeps the letter out of evidence later.
And if I only want to sound reasonable?
Then say you're acting in good faith, and mean it. Both sides can read that phrase in court.
Do we need legal counsel for something this small?
You have legal counsel. I'll draft a contract variation this afternoon, and then we can enforce something clear instead of arguing about an email.

title: Who pays if it falls
setting: A contractor wants a very wide promise before starting work.

lines.t: If the scaffolding fails, who pays?
Whoever was careless. That's negligence, and it follows the facts more than the paperwork.
The contract says they're liable for anything on site.
It says they carry the liability. A court will still ask who actually failed to check it.
So we could still be in it.
If our own people signed off the inspection, yes.
They want an indemnity from us for delays.
For delays we cause, fine. For anything at all, no. An open indemnity is a blank cheque with your signature on it.
What do I say to them?
That we're liable for our own work and that's where it ends. It's a normal position and they'll expect it.

title: Four years of it
setting: A threat arrives over an invoice from 2021.

lines.t: They're threatening to sue.
Over the invoice from 2021?
That one.
Then check the statute of limitations before anybody panics. There may be nothing left to bring.
And if there is?
They'd be the claimant, we'd be the defendant, and litigation would take three years.
What would they ask for?
Damages of about ninety thousand. They'd get considerably less.
Can we avoid a hearing altogether?
The contract sends disputes to arbitration, which is faster and private.
I'd rather settle out of court.
So would they. Nobody enjoys giving testimony about an email they wrote four years ago.
And if the verdict goes against us?
We can appeal, and that costs another year. Which is the real argument for settling in March.

title: The list in the drawer
setting: Marketing has two thousand email addresses and no idea where they came from.

lines.t: Marketing has a list of two thousand email addresses in a drawer.
On paper?
On a memory stick, in a drawer.
Then we have a data protection problem, and the drawer is the smallest part of it.
Where did the list come from?
That's the question the regulator asks first. Nobody collects personal data and decides afterwards why.
The new supplier wants access to our customer records as well.
Not before a non-disclosure agreement, and not without knowing where they store it.
They say everything is confidential.
Everyone says that. We comply with the regulation by writing down what we hold, why we hold it, and for how long.
So compliance is a document.
Compliance is a habit. The document is the part you can show somebody.

title: Before you sign for us
setting: A director will be abroad in the week the papers have to be signed.

lines.t: I'm in Vienna next week and the papers need signing here.
Then give somebody a power of attorney, limited to this transaction.
Can't I email my approval?
The bank won't take it. And the articles of association say two directors sign anything over fifty thousand.
What about the new company we're setting up?
It'll be a subsidiary, wholly owned. Same rules, separate accounts.
Do we need anything from the board?
A board resolution, dated before the signing rather than after it.
And my brother's twenty per cent?
That belongs in a shareholder agreement, written while everybody still likes each other.
And before we buy the Plovdiv business?
Due diligence. Six weeks of it, because I'd rather find the problem than inherit it.

title: Sign first, talk second
setting: A founder learns why the NDA didn't protect them.

lines.t: They launched a copy of our pricing model. Can we sue?
When did you sign the non-disclosure agreement?
In May.
And when did you explain the model to them?
March. Two friendly meetings.
Then it sits outside the agreement. The NDA only covers what came after.
Isn't the model our intellectual property?
A business idea usually isn't. A patent or copyright would be.
That's an expensive lesson.
One sentence long. Sign first, talk second.

title: The logo somebody drew
setting: Nobody checked who owns the company's own logo.

lines.t: A freelancer designed our logo in 2019. Do we own it?
Only if the contract says so. Otherwise the copyright stayed with him.
He was paid.
Payment buys the work. Intellectual property moves only when somebody writes it down.
So what do we do?
Write to him, politely, and agree a transfer or a licence. Most people say yes.
Should we register it as a trademark?
The name first, then the logo. A trademark stops somebody opening the same shop next door under your name.
And the machine Georgi modified?
If it's genuinely new there may be a patent in it. Tell him to stop describing it publicly until we've asked.
